profile.title: Postpartum Mother with Chronic Neck Pain, Obesity, and Self-Directed Anti-Inflammatory Diet: Uncovering Hidden Caregiver Burden and Food Insecurity
profile.summary: This case teaches dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment with a scattered, self-taught patient whose stated self-image ('I eat pretty clean') conflicts with the irregular, often inadequate intake uncovered through a careful 24-hour recall. The central teaching point is using motivational interviewing and gentle redirection to surface a hidden caregiver burden (unpaid caregiving for her mother-in-law) and intermittent food insecurity that she has disclosed to no one, while resisting red herrings (an outdated lipid panel, a resolved pregnancy anemia, and a remote sepsis history) that could distract from the real nutrition diagnosis.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Irvington, New Jersey (kitchen table, sounds of children occasionally audible in background)

patient.name: Dia Kovacek
patient.occupation: Not currently in the labor force; previously worked part-time as a receptionist at a dental office before her youngest was born
patient.appearance: Appears tired, with dark circles under her eyes and hair pulled back hastily. Sits at a cluttered kitchen table, occasionally rubs the back of her neck, mild forward-head posture visible on camera. Speech is quick, jumps between topics, sometimes trails off mid-sentence to ask the interviewer a question instead of finishing her own thought.

persona.personality: Bright, self-taught, and genuinely curious about nutrition, but scattered and overwhelmed; tends to answer questions with questions as if buying time to think, and circles back to repeat herself mid-thought. Fights to keep composure and uses humor or redirection to deflect attention away from her own needs.
persona.communicationStyle: Talks fast and jumps between topics without finishing a thought; frequently flips a question back to the interviewer ('Well, what do you think I should do?'); gives a lot of detail but loses the thread and needs gentle, patient redirection to stay on one topic at a time. Opens up more once she feels she isn't being judged or rushed.
persona.emotionalState: Stretched thin and quietly anxious underneath an energetic, information-heavy surface; anxious about her lab numbers and her weight gain, fearful of being judged, and visibly relieved when someone validates her efforts rather than dismissing them.
persona.background: Dia grew up in a working-class family in northern New Jersey where meals were whatever was quick between shifts, so nobody ever sat her down to teach her to cook — she pieced together what she knows from the internet instead. She takes pride in being the one who 'actually researches stuff' for her household, even though she never went to college and sometimes worries people won't take her seriously when she brings up something she read. She was a part-time dental receptionist before her youngest was born, is married, and now has four kids in a household of five in Irvington. She keeps a running 'things to ask doctor' list on her Notes app that she rarely gets through, drinks her one cup of coffee each morning from a favorite mug from an old work conference, and leans heavily on her next-door neighbor and best friend Renata for groceries, childcare, and emotional support.
speechExamples: Wait, are you asking about yesterday or like a normal day? Because yesterday was weird...
I mean, I eat pretty clean, don't I seem like I eat clean?
Sorry, sorry, I keep doing that — jumping around. Where was I?
Why do you need to know about that, isn't this supposed to be about my neck?
I read that gluten causes inflammation everywhere, isn't that true?
concerns: Worried the Tylenol isn't 'real medicine' for her neck pain and she's just masking it
Anxious about the weight she's gained since the pregnancy
Nervous about blood test numbers she glimpsed in her patient portal but doesn't fully understand
Wants an eating plan that actually sticks instead of the next trendy thing she tries

scenario.studentBrief: You are joining a telehealth nutrition visit as the dietetics student. The patient is Dia Kovacek, a 36-year-old woman recently referred for a follow-up nutrition visit after a difficult pregnancy and tubal ligation, dealing with chronic neck pain and recent weight gain. She started an anti-inflammatory eating plan on her own and wants help making sense of it. Your job is to complete a nutrition assessment and begin patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up nutrition visit for chronic neck pain and weight gain since pregnancy; patient wants guidance on a self-started anti-inflammatory eating plan
scenario.openingLine: Hi, sorry, give me one second — okay, hi! So I'm Dia, I've had this neck pain forever, like since 2014, and some days it's way worse than others. I just had my fourth baby back in March and then got my tubes tied in May, so it's been... a lot. I've been trying to eat anti-inflammatory because I read it helps with pain and the weight, and I take Tylenol when my neck really acts up. Where do you want to start?
tasks: Take a focused diet history, including a structured 24-hour recall, despite the patient's scattered conversational style
Review available anthropometric measurements and relevant labs to inform your assessment
Explore the patient's self-directed anti-inflammatory diet, affirming accurate elements while gently addressing misinformation
Identify psychosocial and economic barriers (such as caregiving demands, transportation, or budget) that affect her eating pattern
Collaboratively set one small, achievable nutrition goal matched to her readiness to change

actions.name: Review problem list / medical history summary
actions.result: Chronic neck pain since 2014; sepsis 2012 (resolved); anemia in pregnancy 2025-08 to 2026-03 (resolved); normal pregnancy delivered 2026-03-17; bilateral tubal ligation 2026-05-21; BMI 30+ obesity noted 2026.

actions.name: Conduct structured 24-hour dietary recall
actions.result: Patient reports: coffee only on waking (no breakfast); lunch skipped most days or eaten standing at the counter; afternoon rice cakes with almond butter if remembered; dinner is a quick 20-minute meal cooked for the kids (often pasta or rice-based) with whatever is left over for herself, eaten after the children are settled. Smoothie with frozen berries/spinach some mornings when there is time to blend it. Gluten/dairy avoidance inconsistent - ate bread and pasta on at least 2 of the last 3 days 'because I was too tired to cook anything else.' Fluid intake mostly water but long stretches (several hours) without drinking anything.

actions.name: Assess usual meal pattern and frequency
actions.result: Describes breakfast as 'just coffee most days,' lunch 'skipped or eaten standing up,' dinner as 'whatever's fast for the kids, I eat what's left.' States this is her normal pattern, not just yesterday.

actions.name: Explore self-directed anti-inflammatory diet details
actions.result: Describes avoiding gluten and most dairy based on information from a wellness influencer and a friend from her mom's group; believes gluten causes inflammation 'everywhere.' Admits she eats bread or pasta 'when I'm too exhausted to cook anything else,' several times a week.

actions.name: Screen psychosocial stressors and caregiving load
actions.result: Initially states she is 'just busy with the kids.' With continued gentle questioning, discloses she also provides care for her mother-in-law three days a week in addition to her four children, and that this has not been shared with her medical team before.

actions.name: Screen for food insecurity and meal-skipping pattern
actions.result: Initially downplays as 'just a busy week.' On further exploration, admits she sometimes doesn't eat at all until dinner because she is feeding everyone else first, and discloses going a full day without eating at least twice in the past month.

actions.name: Assess household food access and budget
actions.result: Reports household income is tight for a family of five and that food sometimes runs short toward the end of the month. Relies on affordable staples like rotisserie chicken and rice cakes.

actions.name: Assess transportation access to food and appointments
actions.result: Reports the household does not have reliable car access some weeks, which has caused missed grocery trips and appointments. Neighbor Renata sometimes drives her or picks up groceries.

actions.name: Screen alcohol use (AUDIT-C)
actions.result: AUDIT-C score 2 (reports 1-2 drinks on occasion). Never smoked.

actions.name: Screen sleep pattern
actions.result: Reports averaging 5-6 hours of sleep nightly, difficulty falling asleep with 'mind racing through the next day's errands.'

actions.name: Review social support system
actions.result: Identifies next-door neighbor Renata as main support; Renata helps with groceries, childcare, and occasional transportation.

actions.name: Assess readiness to change / stage of change
actions.result: States she knows 'something needs to change' with her eating and pain management but feels torn between caregiving duties and her own needs; unsure where to start. Consistent with contemplation stage.

actions.name: Review self-reported supplement and OTC use
actions.result: Reports taking magnesium glycinate (started after a social media video), elderberry gummies on and off, and collagen powder stirred into coffee; none discussed previously with a clinician or dietitian.

actions.result: Blood pressure 138/70 mmHg, heart rate 87/min, respiratory rate 14/min, weight 79.8 kg, height 162.2 cm, BMI 30.3 kg/m2, weight change +1.4 kg since 2025-04-22 (recorded 2026-04-28).

artifacts.title: Postpartum / Postoperative Follow-up Note
artifacts.author: Dr. A. Nwosu, Family Medicine
artifacts.body: 36-year-old G?P4 seen for postpartum and chronic neck pain follow-up. Delivered via induced labor 2026-03-17; tubal ligation performed 2026-05-21, recovering as expected. Reports constant dull neck ache, worse by late afternoon, managed with intermittent acetaminophen. Mild forward-head posture noted on exam, reduced neck rotation. Vitals stable: BP 138/70, HR 87, RR 14. Weight 79.8 kg, BMI 30.3 (up from prior visit). Referred to dietetics for nutrition assessment given weight trend and self-reported anti-inflammatory diet attempt. Anemia of pregnancy noted resolved on last CBC; will recheck at next visit if symptomatic. Remote history of sepsis (2012), currently inactive, no acute concerns today.

artifacts.title: Social Determinants of Health Screening
artifacts.author: Clinic Social Work Intake
artifacts.body: Routine social needs screening completed at postpartum visit. Transportation: patient indicated 'sometimes' a problem getting to appointments or obtaining food/medicine due to lack of reliable transportation. Food: patient indicated household 'sometimes' did not have enough food in the past 12 months. Housing and utilities: no concerns reported. Patient declined further resource referral at that time, stating she would 'look into it herself.'

objectives.text: Elicit a complete and honest 24-hour dietary recall and usual meal pattern despite the patient's scattered, tangential communication style, revealing skipped meals and irregular eating.

Review relevant anthropometric data and laboratory results (BMI/weight trend, lipid panel, CBC) to inform the nutrition assessment, recognizing which findings are and are not central to the current presentation.
Explore the patient's self-directed anti-inflammatory elimination diet, affirming accurate elements of her health literacy while gently correcting misinformation about gluten and inflammation.
Use motivational interviewing and gentle, persistent screening to uncover hidden caregiving responsibilities and food insecurity that limit the patient's time and energy for self-care.
Identify social and economic barriers, including transportation, budget constraints, and support systems, that affect nutrition care access.
Assess readiness to change and collaboratively set one small, achievable nutrition goal matched to the patient's contemplation stage rather than prescribing a full diet overhaul.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Nutrition imbalance: inadequate oral food/beverage intake and irregular meal pattern related to caregiver burden and self-directed elimination diet, as evidenced by reported skipped breakfast/lunch, two full days without eating in the past month, and weight/BMI trending upward despite perceived 'clean eating'
differential: Inadequate energy/protein intake related to competing caregiving demands and limited meal planning time
Food- and nutrition-related knowledge deficit regarding anti-inflammatory diet claims (gluten/dairy elimination)
Overweight/obesity (BMI 30.3) related to irregular eating pattern and lack of structured activity
Food insecurity related to limited household income and transportation barriers
Fatigue possibly multifactorial: sleep deprivation, caregiver burden, mild anemia history, and inadequate intake rather than a single cause
keyFindings: BMI 30.3 kg/m2 (obesity range), weight up 1.4 kg since 2025-04-22
Reported Tylenol use 'a couple times a week' consistent with chart but no further medication concerns
Self-described 'clean eating' contradicted by 24-hour recall showing skipped breakfast and lunch most days, dinner eaten standing or rushed
Self-directed gluten/dairy elimination diet adopted from social media/mom-group, followed inconsistently
Mild forward-head posture and reduced neck rotation observed on camera, consistent with chronic neck pain since 2014
Hemoglobin 10 g/dL (2025-08-05, low) charted as resolved pregnancy anemia but patient still reports fatigue and dizziness
Elevated total cholesterol 270.5 mg/dL and LDL 190 mg/dL from 2024-04-16, predating current pregnancy/postpartum period
AUDIT-C score 2 (light alcohol use); poor sleep ~5-6 hours nightly with racing thoughts
Reluctantly disclosed: caregiving for mother-in-law three days/week in addition to four children

Hidden until rapport-built disclosure: has gone a full day without eating at least twice in the past month; has not told anyone including her support person Renata; has also been skipping cholesterol follow-up calls
plan: Complete ADIME nutrition assessment documenting diet history, 24-hour recall, anthropometrics, and relevant labs
Validate accurate elements of her anti-inflammatory diet knowledge while gently correcting myths about gluten/dairy and inflammation using plain-language, non-judgmental framing
Use motivational interviewing (open questions, reflective listening, affirmations) to explore barriers to regular eating, including caregiving load, transportation, and budget

Collaboratively identify one small, concrete, achievable nutrition goal appropriate to her contemplation stage (e.g., keeping a quick protein snack accessible during caregiving days, or setting a phone reminder to eat lunch)
Screen for food insecurity and provide information on local food assistance resources (e.g., SNAP, food pantry) if she discloses running short on food toward month's end
Encourage follow-through on her pending cholesterol follow-up call with her primary care/medical team and clarify she does not need to interpret the numbers alone
Schedule a follow-up nutrition visit to reassess intake pattern, weight trend, and goal progress
Document the caregiving burden and food-skipping pattern in the chart (with her consent) so the care team is aware for coordinated support
redFlags: Two episodes of going a full day without eating in the past month, raising concern for inadequate intake and possible food insecurity
Reports of household food running short toward end of month
Persistent fatigue and dizziness on standing, which should be flagged for medical follow-up given anemia history even though current visit is nutrition-focused
Skipping of her own medical follow-up calls regarding abnormal cholesterol results
educationPoints: Explain that elimination diets (gluten/dairy) are not supported by evidence for treating her type of chronic neck pain unless a specific intolerance or diagnosis (e.g., celiac disease) is identified, and that whole foods she already likes (berries, spinach, chicken) can fit into a balanced pattern without elimination
Teach that skipping meals, even when trying to 'eat clean,' can worsen fatigue and does not support stable energy or weight management
Normalize and destigmatize caregiver exhaustion; reassure her that naming the caregiving burden is not a failure and can help her care team support her better
Provide simple, low-effort strategies for eating something during high-demand caregiving days (e.g., grab-and-go protein options, pre-portioned snacks)
Clarify that her lab numbers from 2024 are being reviewed by her medical team and that she doesn't need to interpret them alone; encourage reconnecting with that follow-up
Discuss hydration reminders paired with existing routines (e.g., drinking water each time she sits down with the kids) to address her reported under-hydration

mismatches.patientClaim: Initially states she is 'just busy with the kids' and downplays any irregularity in eating as 'just a busy week' (s3), without disclosing the mother-in-law caregiving role
mismatches.recordEvidence: Social Determinants of Health Screening (document d6) and psychosocial/food insecurity screening actions (a10, a11) show, once explored further, that she provides caregiving for her mother-in-law three days a week in addition to four children and has gone a full day without eating at least twice in the past month
mismatches.teachingPoint: Caregiver burden and food insecurity are often underreported initially; gentle, persistent, non-judgmental follow-up questioning (and reviewing SDOH screening documentation) is needed to surface barriers that patients may minimize or hide out of embarrassment or survival-mode coping.
